preamble: Vocalization of a voiced velar to a high back rounded vocoid, usually the offglide [u̯] of a new diphthong. In Middle English, Old English g after back vowels and before vowels or liquids, pronounced as the fricative [ɣ], became [w] and then the second element of a diphthong (OE boga > ME bowe > bow). The outcome is a non-syllabic [u̯], overlapping with the g → w cell.

examples.to: Middle English foul, fowel, English fowl
examples.note: Middle English variant foghel keeps the fricative; foul shows full vocalization

examples.to: Middle English drauen, drawen, English draw

examples.from: Old English lagu (from Old Norse lǫg)
examples.note: Middle English laȝe keeps the fricative spelling

sources: Hogg, R. M. (Ed.) (1992). The Cambridge History of the English Language, Vol. 1: The Beginnings to 1066. Cambridge University Press.
